name: The Aran Islands
tagline: Three small, wind-scoured islands off Galway Bay, still Irish-speaking, still walled in stone, and still a step back in time.
highlight: Standing at the unguarded edge of Dún Aengus, a 2,000-year-old fort perched on a sheer 100-metre cliff, with nothing but a drop to the Atlantic below.
shortDescription: Three small, Irish-speaking islands off Galway Bay, criss-crossed with stone walls and home to Dún Aengus, a dramatic Iron Age cliff-edge fort.
metaDescription: An Aran Islands travel guide: Dún Aengus, Kilronan, the Seven Churches, food and how to plan a visit to Inis Mór and Ireland's Irish-speaking islands.
nearestAirport: Shannon Airport (SNN), or fly directly to the islands from Connemara Airport
knownFor: Dún Aengus, stone walls, traditional Aran sweaters

intro: The Aran Islands are a step back in time, three small islands off Galway Bay where Irish remains the everyday language and a dense network of stone walls still divides the fields, built by hand over centuries from cleared limestone.
Inis Mór, the largest, is home to Dún Aengus, a dramatic Iron Age stone fort perched right on the edge of a sheer 100-metre cliff, with no barrier between visitors and the drop.

Most visitors take the ferry from Galway or Doolin as a day trip, though staying overnight allows real time to cycle the island's quiet lanes at an unhurried pace, well after the day-trippers have left.

whyVisit.intro: The Aran Islands' case rests on real remoteness and a living connection to old Irish culture found nowhere else.

points.title: Dún Aengus is one of Ireland's most dramatic ancient sites
points.text: A 2,000-year-old fort on a sheer cliff edge, with no barrier between visitors and the Atlantic below.

points.title: Irish is still the everyday language here
points.text: One of Ireland's strongest Gaeltacht regions, not a tourist performance of the language.

points.title: The stone walls are a landscape in themselves
points.text: Thousands of kilometres of hand-built walls dividing tiny fields cleared from bare limestone.

points.title: It's quiet once the day-trip ferries leave
points.text: An overnight stay reveals a much slower, quieter island than the daytime crowds suggest.

points.title: The traditional Aran sweater originates here
points.text: A distinctive hand-knit style with patterns once said to identify individual island families.

attractionsIntro: Inis Mór's essential sights combine ancient forts with a still-living traditional culture.

attractions.name: Dún Aengus

image.alt: Dún Aengus, an Iron Age stone fort on Inis Mór

attractions.text: One of Ireland's most dramatic ancient sites, a 2,000-year-old fort on the edge of a sheer 100-metre cliff, with the semicircular walls open to the drop.
attractions.tip: Stay well back from the unguarded cliff edge — there is no barrier at all.

attractions.name: The cliffs at Dún Aonghasa

image.file: File:Cliffs at Dún Aonghasa • Dun Aengus (41231272755).jpg
image.alt: The sheer cliffs below Dún Aengus on Inis Mór

attractions.text: A vertigo-inducing view straight down the cliff face from the fort's edge, among Ireland's most striking natural drops.
attractions.tip: Lie flat and crawl to the very edge if you want the full drop in view — many visitors do.

attractions.name: Kilronan village

image.file: File:The harbour at Kilronan on the Aran Islands - geograph.org.uk - 7862768.jpg
image.alt: Kilronan harbour, the main village on Inis Mór

attractions.text: The islands' main village and ferry port, a small, easy base with shops, pubs and bike rental right at the harbour.
attractions.tip: Rent a bike here on arrival — it's the best way to see the rest of the island.

attractions.name: Inis Mór's stone walls

image.file: File:Stone Walls and Ocean Light, Inis Mór, Aran Islands.jpg
image.alt: The dense network of stone walls covering Inis Mór

attractions.text: A landscape in themselves, thousands of kilometres of hand-built dry-stone walls dividing tiny fields cleared from bare limestone.
attractions.tip: Look closely at the wall construction — many are loosely stacked on purpose, to let storm winds pass through.

attractions.name: The Seven Churches

image.alt: The ruins of the Seven Churches on Inis Mór

attractions.text: An atmospheric early Christian monastic site, despite the name actually comprising two churches and several other ruined structures.
attractions.tip: Quieter than Dún Aengus — a peaceful stop away from the main crowds.

attractions.name: Aran sweater shops

image.file: File:Aran Sweater Market in Kilronan, Inishmore (2014).jpg
image.alt: A shop selling traditional Aran sweaters in Kilronan

attractions.text: The origin of the famous hand-knit style, with distinctive stitch patterns and a history tied closely to the islands.
attractions.tip: Look for a hand-knit label if authenticity matters to you — many cheaper versions are machine-made elsewhere.

attractions.name: Traditional currach boats

image.alt: A traditional currach boat on the Aran Islands

attractions.text: Still used by some island fishermen, lightweight canvas-and-tar boats built to a design centuries old.
attractions.tip: Look for currachs drawn up near Kilronan harbour or smaller landing spots around the island.

thingsToDoIntro: Inis Mór rewards a full day on a bike, covering the island at an unhurried, human pace.

thingsToDo.title: Cycle Inis Mór's quiet lanes

image.alt: A quiet road crossing the centre of Inis Mór

thingsToDo.text: The best way to see the island, pedalling between stone-walled fields with barely any traffic to worry about.
thingsToDo.tip: Rent a bike at Kilronan harbour on arrival — no booking needed outside peak summer.

thingsToDo.title: Walk up to Dún Aengus

image.file: File:Way to Dún Aonghasa • Dun Aengus (27262045747).jpg
image.alt: The path leading up to Dún Aengus fort

thingsToDo.text: A moderate uphill walk from the visitor centre, rewarded by one of Ireland's most dramatic ancient sites.
thingsToDo.tip: Wear sturdy shoes — the final stretch crosses uneven limestone.

thingsToDo.title: Explore the Seven Churches

image.file: File:Na Seacht dTeampaill • The Seven Churches (41412428344).jpg
image.alt: The ruined Seven Churches monastic site on Inis Mór

thingsToDo.text: A quieter, atmospheric stop away from the main Dún Aengus crowds, easily reached by bike.
thingsToDo.tip: Combine with a stop at the nearby beach for a full, relaxed afternoon.

thingsToDo.title: Shop for a genuine Aran sweater

image.alt: A traditional hand-knit Aran sweater

thingsToDo.text: A worthwhile souvenir with real history, distinctive stitch patterns once said to identify individual families.
thingsToDo.tip: Ask about hand-knit versus machine-made if authenticity and craft matter to your purchase.

thingsToDo.title: Photograph the island's abandoned cottages

image.file: File:Abandoned house on Inishmore, Co. Galway (2014).jpg
image.alt: An abandoned stone cottage on Inis Mór

thingsToDo.text: An evocative, if slightly melancholy, part of cycling the island, passing stone cottages left empty by past emigration.
thingsToDo.tip: Respect that these are on private land — photograph from the road rather than entering.

thingsToDo.title: Watch a traditional currach on the water

image.alt: A traditional Irish currach boat on the water

thingsToDo.text: A rare, living link to the islands' fishing heritage, still occasionally seen worked by local rowers.
thingsToDo.tip: Ask locally about any currach races timed around your visit, held some summer weekends.

accommodation.intro: Kilronan serves as the islands' main base, small but sufficient for an overnight stay.

areas.name: Kilronan
areas.bestFor: Being close to the ferry and bike rental
areas.text: The most practical base, with the islands' main concentration of guesthouses and restaurants.

areas.name: Elsewhere on Inis Mór
areas.text: A handful of guesthouses further from Kilronan offer real solitude, reachable by bike or the island's minibus.

gettingThere.intro: The Aran Islands are reachable only by ferry or small plane, never by road.

options.text: The most common route, with regular sailings, especially in summer.
options.detail: Crossing takes around 40 minutes to an hour and a half depending on departure point.

options.text: A popular option for visitors coming from the Cliffs of Moher direction.
options.detail: A seasonal route, weather-dependent like all island sailings.

options.text: A fast, scenic alternative, taking only a few minutes in the air.
options.detail: A memorable, if pricier, way to reach the islands.

gettingAround.intro: Inis Mór is best explored by bike, with a few alternatives for those who prefer not to cycle.

options.text: The most popular and rewarding way to see the island, available right at Kilronan harbour.
options.detail: Covers Dún Aengus, the Seven Churches and the island's main sights comfortably in a day.

options.text: A practical option for those unable or unwilling to cycle.

bestTime.headline: May, June and September for good weather and thinner crowds
bestTime.summary: The islands are visitable through the warmer months, with far fewer sailings and services outside the main season.

seasons.text: Mild weather with noticeably thinner crowds than midsummer.
The busiest season, with the widest choice of ferry sailings and the most day-trippers.
A quiet, often mild window with fewer visitors than summer.
Limited ferry services and a real chance of sailings being cancelled for weather.

bestTime.avoid: Booking a winter day trip without a flexible schedule — check ferry status closely, since sailings are weather-dependent.

tipsIntro: Practical notes that make an Aran Islands visit noticeably smoother.
tips: Book ferry tickets ahead in summer, and check the weather — sailings depend on conditions.
Rent a bike right at Kilronan harbour on arrival, no advance booking usually needed.
Stay well back from Dún Aengus's unguarded cliff edge.
Consider an overnight stay to see the island once the day-trip crowds leave.
Pack a proper windproof layer regardless of season — the islands are exposed.
Bring some cash — card acceptance is less consistent than on the mainland.

faq.q: How many days do you need on the Aran Islands?
faq.a: A single day covers Kilronan and Dún Aengus, though an overnight allows for a much quieter, more relaxed visit.

faq.q: Can you visit the Aran Islands as a day trip?
faq.a: Yes — it's a popular day trip from Galway or Doolin, with regular ferries in season.

faq.q: Is Dún Aengus safe to visit?
faq.a: Yes, with sensible caution — the cliff edge itself is unguarded, so visitors need to stay well back and supervise children closely.

faq.q: Do people still speak Irish on the Aran Islands?
faq.a: Yes — the islands are one of Ireland's strongest Gaeltacht, or Irish-speaking, regions, with the language used in daily life.

faq.q: What is the best way to get around Inis Mór?
faq.a: By bike, rented right at Kilronan harbour — it covers the island's main sights comfortably in a day.

faq.q: Where does the Aran sweater come from?
faq.a: From these islands — the distinctive hand-knit style originates here, with stitch patterns historically tied to individual island families.
